title: Borrowed Time

pages.text:
The sun hung low and orange, painting the grey mudflats in shades of apricot and rust. It was Day Nine. The air smelled of brine and impending magic. Juno stood at the edge of the harbor, her yellow raincoat bright against the dull landscape. She clutched the spiral shell whistle. It was warm, almost hot, like a stone left in the sun all day.

"I'm going alone," she whispered to herself. Her voice shook, but her hands did not.

Behind her, Teo adjusted his round glasses, his messy black hair sticking up despite his green cap. He held the Storm Bell tightly against his chest. It was heavy, cold, and smelled of rain. "You're going to get caught," he said. "Again. And this time, there will be no cupboard to hide in."

Juno looked at him. He looked terrified. Not of the water, today. Of failure.

"If I bring the bell," Juno said softly, "I can't listen. The bell is loud. The gear needs quiet."

Teo frowned, his lips pressed into a thin line. "It’s a gear. It’s metal. It doesn’t care about listening."

"It’s part of the Clock," Juno insisted. "It breathes. I can hear it trying to turn. It’s lonely."

Barnacle, tucked safely inside Juno’s pocket, poked his long, feathery antennae out. "Honestly! The child has a point. The gear is dramatic. It likes attention. But mostly, it likes being put back where it belongs."

Teo sighed, a long, rattling sound. He looked at the silver car parked by the fish market, gleaming under the dying light. He looked at his own hands, which were still wet from the pier. Then, slowly, he nodded.

"Go," he said. "But if you come back with a ticket, I’m throwing the bell into the bay."

Juno smiled, a small, fragile thing. "Deal." She turned and walked toward the silver car, her boots squelching in the mud. The sea was silent, but she could feel it watching.
pages.image: A view from the muddy shore looking toward a gleaming silver car parked near a fish market; a girl in a bright yellow raincoat walks away from the camera, carrying a shell, while a boy in a green cap watches from the background, holding a large brass bell.

pages.text:
The silver car was a smooth, cold beast. It sat in the gravel lot, its windows dark and reflective. Juno stopped ten feet away. She could see her own reflection in the door: two puffs of curly dark-brown hair, freckles, eyes wide with fear.

She didn’t shout. She didn’t bang on the glass. She took a deep breath, the kind that pulled her belly tight, and she listened.

The whistle in her hand hummed. It wasn’t a sound, exactly. It was a vibration, a low thrum that traveled up her arm and settled in her chest. The air around the car seemed to thicken. The dust motes in the evening light slowed down, hanging suspended.

The driver’s side door opened.

Mr. Cornelius Grubb stepped out. He was tall and thin, his shiny grey suit unwrinkled, his tiny mustache perfectly trimmed. He looked at Juno, then at the empty street, then back at her.

"Miss Vale," he said. His voice was smooth, like oil. "You’re back. I expected you to be crying, or running. Not standing there looking like you’re about to negotiate a treaty."

Juno didn’t move. "I’m not here to negotiate, Mr. Grubb."

"Then why are you here?"

"Because you have something that doesn’t belong to you."

Grubb’s eyes narrowed. He shifted his weight, his polished shoes clicking on the gravel. "I have many things that don’t belong to you. My time. My patience. My parking spot." He gestured vaguely at the car. "What do you want, child?"

Juno thought of the glass case in his office, and of the Moon Gear sitting on its velvet cushion, a small, perfect circle of brass. It had looked dead. It had looked like a toy.

"Tell me why you took it," Juno said.
pages.image: A close-up of a man in a grey suit standing by a silver car, looking sternly at a girl in a yellow raincoat who is holding a shell; the car's reflection shows the girl's anxious face, and the background is a dusty, empty parking lot at dusk.

pages.text:
Grubb stared at her. For a moment, his professional mask slipped. His jaw tightened. He looked tired. Not the tiredness of a long day, but the deep, bone-weariness of someone who had been holding a wall up for a very long time.

"Why do I take things?" he repeated. He let out a short, dry laugh. "Because when I was small, I had nothing. Not even a lake."

Juno waited. The silence stretched between them.

"My father had a boat," Grubb said, his voice dropping. He looked at the water, or the mud where the water used to be. "A little blue rowboat. We lived on a lake. It was beautiful. But the water went away. Not all at once. Just... slowly. One day, the boat was on grass. The next day, it was on dirt. And then, it was just a boat on a hill."

He shuddered, a tiny, involuntary movement.

"I was seven. I thought I had done something wrong. I thought if I was quiet, if I was good, the water would come back. It didn’t. So I learned something. If you can’t control the water, you control the land. You buy it. You pave it. You make it safe. You make it predictable." He looked back at Juno. "I didn’t know what that gear was. I saw a valuable antique part in a broken lighthouse. I took it because I was afraid it would be sold for scrap. I wanted to keep it. To keep it safe. Like the boat."

Juno felt a pang of sadness. He wasn’t a monster. He was just scared.

"I know," she said.

Grubb blinked. "You know?"

"You’re afraid of being poor again," Juno said gently. "Afraid of losing what you have."

He didn’t argue. He just looked down at his shoes.
pages.image: A man in a grey suit standing by his car, looking down at his polished shoes, his expression sad and tired; in the background, the muddy harbor is visible, and the lighting is soft and golden, suggesting a late afternoon.

pages.text:
"Can I show you something?" Juno asked.

Grubb hesitated. He wanted to say no. He wanted to get back in his car and drive away from this strange, stubborn girl. But the air was still thick with that humming vibration.

"Show me," he said.

Juno took a step closer. She didn’t reach for the gear. Instead, she held up the shell whistle. She didn’t blow it. She just held it out, letting the warmth radiate from it.

"Listen," she said.

Grubb frowned. "I’m listening to you."

"No. Listen to the sea."

Grubb looked at the muddy shore. "The sea is gone, child. You know this."

"Not gone," Juno said. "Waiting."

She turned to the side of the car. There, in the gravel, was a small puddle of rainwater, left over from the storm earlier. It was clear and still. Juno pointed to it.

"Look at the water," she said.

Grubb crouched down. He was a man in a grey suit, kneeling in the dirt. It looked ridiculous. He looked into the puddle.

At first, he saw only his own reflection: his grey suit, his mustache, his worry. But then, the reflection changed. The water rippled, though there was no wind. The image in the puddle shifted, becoming deep and blue. He saw the shadow of a giant, elegant shell. He heard a sound, low and resonant, like a cello playing in a distant room.

It was the voice of the Deep Court. It was the voice of the sea, calling out to him.

Grubb gasped. He stared at the puddle, his eyes wide. "What... what is that?"

"That’s the tide," Juno said. "It’s not angry. It’s just trying to tell you something. The gear belongs to the Clock. The Clock belongs to the sea. If you keep the gear, you keep the sea away. You keep the mud."

Grubb’s hand trembled. He reached into his pocket and pulled out a small key.
pages.image: A man in a grey suit kneeling in the dirt next to a silver car, staring into a small puddle of water that reflects a deep blue ocean and a large nautilus shell; a girl in a yellow raincoat stands beside him, watching his reaction.

pages.text:
He unlocked the driver’s side door. He didn’t get in. Instead, he walked to the trunk and popped it open. Inside, wrapped in a velvet cloth, was the Moon Gear. He had been carrying it around all day, he admitted later, because he could not stand to leave it alone in the empty office.

He picked it up. It was heavier than he expected. In his hand, it didn’t look like a valuable antique. It looked like a piece of a puzzle that had been taken from a very old, very important machine.

"I don't understand it," Grubb said, his voice rough. "I don't understand how it works. I don't understand why it matters to you. But..." He looked at the puddle. The blue reflection was fading, but the echo of the deep voice still lingered in the air. "But I remember the boat. And I remember the silence."

He extended his hand. The gear sat in his palm, gleaming in the last light of the day.

Juno reached out. Her fingers brushed his. His hand was cold, but steady. He let go.

The gear settled into Juno’s palm. It was warm. It hummed. It felt like a heartbeat.

"Thank you," Juno whispered.

"Don't thank me," Grubb said, straightening up. He smoothed his suit, his face returning to its usual smooth mask, but his eyes were different. Softer. "Just... make sure it works. I'd hate to think I kept it for nothing."

Juno nodded. She tucked the gear into her pocket, next to the shell whistle. The vibration was stronger now. The sea was close.

"Tonight," Juno said, "we go to the lighthouse."

Grubb looked at the horizon, where the stars were beginning to appear. "Tonight," he repeated. He got into his car. The door closed with a soft *thud*. He started the engine, but he didn’t drive away. He sat there, watching Juno walk back toward the harbor.

Juno walked with a new confidence. The bell was with Teo. The gear was with her. The sea was listening. And the clock was waiting.
pages.image: A girl in a yellow raincoat walking away from a silver car, holding a small brass gear in her hand; a man in a grey suit sits in the driver's seat, watching her go; the background is a darkening sky with the first stars appearing.

summary: Juno confronts Mr. Grubb at his car and listens to his fear of poverty and loss, which stems from a childhood memory of a dried-up lake. By using the shell whistle to reveal the voice of the sea in a puddle, she shows him that the Moon Gear belongs to the natural world, not his office. Grubb returns the gear, acknowledging the power of the tide, and Juno leaves with the final piece needed for the Tide Clock.
